readerContract.humanQuestion: Will AI data centers now have to pay for upgrades instead of raising my household electricity bill?
readerContract.answer: No change to a household bill follows from this House vote alone. The bill describes a standard that state utility authorities would consider if it became law; it does not promise a bill reduction.
readerContract.mentalModel: A bill can direct regulators to consider a rate standard without setting your utility rate or forcing one immediate result.

unadmittedResearchWording.headline: The House passed a data-center power bill. Your electricity rate did not change.
unadmittedResearchWording.theStory:
The U.S. House passed H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, 417–3 on September 16. The House-approved text concerns very large, non-residential customers: sites using at least 100 megawatts for data-storage and computing systems.

If it became law, the proposal would ask state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider a standard designed to make those large customers cover the full incremental cost of upgrades needed to serve them. It gives those bodies time to consider and decide; it does not set a new rate for every utility customer.
unadmittedResearchWording.whatThisMeans:
Your electricity bill did not change because of this House vote. Whether a utility passes infrastructure costs through to households depends on utility regulation and local rate decisions. This bill is aimed at the question of who pays for upgrades tied to a very large new customer, but it does not guarantee lower bills.

There is also no final federal law in the material reviewed here. The Government Publishing Office record is the House-engrossed version. The American Public Power Association reports that a September 17 unanimous-consent Senate attempt drew an objection; this draft attributes that report and does not claim a complete Senate docket.
unadmittedResearchWording.readerAction: When you see a claim that a data center will raise or lower local rates, ask which utility commission sets the rate, which upgrade is at issue, and whether the claim describes a proposal, a regulator's decision, or an actual bill.

claimLimits: Do not say the bill was enacted, that the Senate passed it, or that there is a complete current official Senate status.
Do not call it an immediate national rule, a mandatory nationwide payment, or a guaranteed household-bill reduction.
Use the 100-megawatt threshold only for the House text's defined large-load customer.
Attribute the September 17 Senate objection to APPA.
requiredNextSteps: Pass the producer contract against this evidence before writing a new draft. The preserved research wording above is not a valid draft and cannot be admitted post hoc.
Create and admit an exact non-character editorial hero visual showing household meter/rate context and a distinct large-load campus; do not use a generic data-center image or publish with no image.
Run the producer self-review, independent review and admission only after the new contract-first draft exists and normal Claude reviewer authentication is restored.
Before any promotion, recover an official Senate action record or retain the APPA attribution and have the final reviewer assess whether that limitation is clear enough.
